Energy Changes.intro: Chemical reactions involve energy changes. Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings.
Energy Changes.mnemonic: EXothermic = EXits heat (temperature goes UP). ENdothermic = ENters heat (temperature goes DOWN). Think: EX = Exit, EN = Enter.

sections.title: Exothermic Reactions
sections.text: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, causing the temperature to rise. Products have less energy stored than reactants.
points: Energy released — transferred to the surroundings; temperature INCREASES
Products have less energy than reactants — energy has left the system
Examples — combustion, neutralisation, respiration, oxidation, hand warmers
ΔH is negative — e.g. ΔH = −890 kJ/mol for methane combustion
Energy profile — products drawn lower than reactants on diagram
Applications — hand warmers use exothermic reactions between iron powder and oxygen

sections.title: Endothermic Reactions
sections.text: Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings, causing the temperature to fall. Products have more energy stored than reactants.
points: Energy absorbed — taken in from surroundings; temperature DECREASES
Products have more energy than reactants — energy has entered the system
Examples — thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate, sports cold packs
ΔH is positive — e.g. ΔH = +178 kJ/mol for thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
Energy profile — products drawn higher than reactants on diagram
Sports cold packs — dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic, absorbing heat from the injury

sections.title: Energy Profile Diagrams
sections.text: Energy profiles show how the energy of the system changes during a reaction, including the activation energy barrier and the overall ΔH.
points: Activation energy (Ea) — the energy barrier; measured from reactants to the peak
ΔH — overall energy change; measured from reactants to products
Exothermic profile — products are lower than reactants; ΔH is negative
Endothermic profile — products are higher than reactants; ΔH is positive
Catalyst effect — lowers the peak (activation energy) but does not change the level of reactants or products
Calorimetry — experimental method to measure energy changes using Q = mcΔT

callout.label: Key Features
callout.text: All energy profiles show: reactants, products, activation energy (peak), overall energy change (ΔH). Exothermic: products lower. Endothermic: products higher.

keyTerms.def: Reaction that releases energy to the surroundings — temperature increases; ΔH is negative
Reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings — temperature decreases; ΔH is positive
Minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur — the peak on an energy profile diagram
The overall energy change of a reaction; negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic
Experimental technique for measuring heat energy transferred using Q = mcΔT
A graph showing how the energy of the reacting system changes from reactants through the transition state to products

examTips: Exothermic = temperature UP (energy OUT to surroundings). Endothermic = temperature DOWN (energy IN from surroundings). Always state the direction of energy transfer.
On energy profiles: activation energy is measured from reactants to the peak. ΔH is from reactants to products — do not mix these up.
In 6-mark questions on evaluating energy experiments, always mention heat loss to the surroundings as a source of error and suggest using insulation/a lid to improve accuracy.
When using Q = mcΔT in the exam: m is in grams, c = 4.18 J/g°C for water, ΔT is the temperature change. Show all steps clearly.
commonMistakes: Saying exothermic reactions have a temperature decrease — it's the opposite; exothermic reactions release energy so the surroundings get warmer.
Confusing activation energy (reactants to peak) with ΔH (reactants to products) on energy profile diagrams.
Drawing the catalyst on an energy profile as changing the height of reactants or products — catalysts only lower the activation energy peak.
clozePassages: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to increase. Examples include combustion, neutralisation, and respiration. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, causing the temperature to decrease. Examples include thermal decomposition and the reaction between citric acid and sodium hydrogen carbonate. In both types, energy is transferred as heat.

An energy level diagram shows the energy of reactants and products in a reaction. In an exothermic reaction, the products have less energy than the reactants — energy is released. In an endothermic reaction, the products have more energy than the reactants — energy is absorbed. The difference in energy is the enthalpy change. The activation energy is the minimum energy needed for the reaction to start.

Energy changes in chemical reactions can be measured using a simple calorimeter. The temperature change of a known mass of water is measured and used to calculate the energy transferred. The formula is: Q = mc∆T, where m is mass, c is specific heat capacity, and ∆T is the temperature change. This technique is used to compare the energy content of fuels and the heat released by neutralisation reactions.

Bond Energies.intro: During reactions, bonds in reactants break (requiring energy) and new bonds form in products (releasing energy). The overall energy change depends on the difference.
Bond Energies.mnemonic: Breaking Bonds = Big effort needed (endothermic). Making bonds = Magnificent energy released (exothermic). BBB-MMM: Break Bonds Big, Make bonds Magnificent!

sections.title: Bond Breaking and Making
sections.text: Energy must be supplied to break bonds (endothermic) and is released when new bonds form (exothermic). The net energy change determines whether the reaction is exo- or endothermic overall.
points: Breaking bonds — ENDOTHERMIC; energy must be INPUT to overcome the attractive forces
Making bonds — EXOTHERMIC; energy is RELEASED as attractive forces form between atoms
Exothermic overall — energy released making bonds > energy needed breaking bonds
Endothermic overall — energy needed breaking bonds > energy released making bonds
Bond energy units — measured in kJ/mol; represent energy to break one mole of that bond
Average bond energies — values are averages across many molecules; give approximate ΔH values

sections.title: Calculating Energy Changes
sections.text: To calculate ΔH using bond energies: sum all energy needed to break bonds in reactants, then subtract all energy released making bonds in products.
points: Step 1 — list all bonds broken in the reactants and their bond energies (kJ/mol)
Step 2 — list all bonds formed in the products and their bond energies (kJ/mol)
Step 3 — ΔH = Σ(energy in to break bonds) − Σ(energy out making bonds)
Negative ΔH — more energy released than absorbed = exothermic reaction
Positive ΔH — more energy absorbed than released = endothermic reaction
Worked example — H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: break H-H (436) + Cl-Cl (243) = 679 kJ in; make 2×H-Cl (2×432 = 864 kJ out); ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol (exothermic)

callout.label: Method
callout.text: 1. List all bonds broken (reactants) and their energies. 2. List all bonds formed (products) and their energies. 3. ΔH = Σ(energy in) − Σ(energy out). Negative answer = exothermic.

sections.title: Common Bond Energies to Know
sections.text: Knowing approximate bond energies helps you tackle calculation questions confidently in the exam.
points: C-H bond — approximately 413 kJ/mol; very common in organic molecules
C=C double bond — approximately 614 kJ/mol; stronger than single C-C (347 kJ/mol)
O=O bond — approximately 498 kJ/mol; in oxygen gas O₂
O-H bond — approximately 464 kJ/mol; in water molecules
C=O bond — approximately 805 kJ/mol (in CO₂); very strong double bond
H-H bond — approximately 436 kJ/mol; in hydrogen gas H₂

keyTerms.def: The energy required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in the gaseous state; measured in kJ/mol
An endothermic process — energy must be supplied to overcome the forces holding atoms together
An exothermic process — energy is released as atoms are held together by new bonds
The overall energy change of a reaction: ΔH = energy in (breaking) − energy out (making)
The mean energy required to break a particular type of bond, averaged across many different molecules
A reaction where more energy is released making bonds than is needed to break bonds; ΔH is negative

examTips: Bond breaking = endothermic (energy IN). Bond making = exothermic (energy OUT). This is a very common exam question — state it clearly.
Show all working in bond energy calculations — list every bond broken and formed separately with its energy value. Examiners award method marks.
Remember to count ALL bonds including the correct number based on subscripts (e.g. CH₄ has 4 C-H bonds; 2H₂O has 4 O-H bonds total).
If ΔH is negative, the reaction is exothermic. If positive, it is endothermic. Always state which type it is as part of your answer.
commonMistakes: Reversing bond breaking and making — breaking bonds always requires energy (endothermic); making bonds always releases energy (exothermic).
Forgetting to multiply bond energies by the number of bonds — e.g. 2H₂O means 4 O-H bonds, not 2.
Not counting bonds in all molecules on both sides of the equation — always draw out the full structural formula mentally to count bonds accurately.
clozePassages: Chemical reactions involve breaking bonds in reactants and forming bonds in products. Breaking bonds is an endothermic process — it requires energy input. Forming bonds is an exothermic process — it releases energy. The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the difference between the energy required to break bonds and the energy released when new bonds form.

If more energy is released forming bonds than is required to break them, the reaction is exothermic. If more energy is required to break bonds than is released forming them, the reaction is endothermic. Bond energies are measured in kJ/mol and represent the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond. Using bond energies allows the overall energy change of a gaseous reaction to be estimated.

The bond energy calculation method: add up the energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants, then subtract the energy released forming all bonds in the products. If the result is negative, the reaction is exothermic (more energy released than taken in). If positive, the reaction is endothermic. This method gives approximate values because bond energies are averages — actual values depend on the molecular environment of each bond.

Fuel Cells.intro: Fuel cells generate electricity directly from a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen, without combustion. The hydrogen fuel cell is the key example for GCSE.
Fuel Cells.mnemonic: Fuel cells: H₂ goes to the Anode (A comes before C), O₂ goes to the Cathode. HAO-C: Hydrogen At the Anode, Oxygen at the Cathode. Only Water produced!

sections.title: How Hydrogen Fuel Cells Work
sections.text: A hydrogen fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy through an electrochemical reaction, producing only water as a by-product.
points: Hydrogen at the anode — H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation — loses electrons)
Electrons flow through the external circuit — this is the electrical current that powers devices
Oxygen at the cathode — O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (reduction — gains electrons)
Overall reaction — hydrogen + oxygen → water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O)
No combustion — direct electrochemical conversion is more efficient than burning
Electrolyte membrane — allows H⁺ ions to pass through but not electrons

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.text: Fuel cells have significant environmental benefits but also real-world challenges around hydrogen production and storage.
points: Advantage: only water produced — no CO₂ or pollutant emissions at the point of use
Advantage: high efficiency — converts chemical energy directly to electrical; no energy lost as heat in combustion
Advantage: continuous supply — unlike batteries, works as long as fuel is supplied; does not need recharging
Disadvantage: hydrogen storage — H₂ is explosive and difficult to store safely under pressure
Disadvantage: hydrogen production — most H₂ is currently made from natural gas (steam reforming), releasing CO₂
Disadvantage: cost and infrastructure — fuel cell technology and hydrogen refuelling stations are expensive

sections.title: Comparison with Batteries and Combustion Engines
sections.text: Fuel cells compare favourably to alternatives in efficiency and emissions, but face practical hurdles in widespread adoption.
points: vs batteries — fuel cells don't run down; batteries store finite charge and must be recharged
vs combustion engines — fuel cells produce no CO₂ at point of use; engines emit CO₂ and other pollutants
Renewable H₂ — if hydrogen is made by electrolysis using renewable electricity, fuel cells are truly zero-emission
Current use — used in some buses, cars (Toyota Mirai), and as backup power generators
Green hydrogen — the future goal; requires large amounts of renewable electricity for electrolysis
Overall verdict — promising technology but dependent on clean H₂ supply to be truly sustainable

keyTerms.def: A device that converts chemical energy from a fuel directly into electrical energy via an electrochemical reaction
A fuel cell where H₂ and O₂ react electrochemically to produce water and electricity
The negative electrode in a fuel cell where hydrogen is oxidised (loses electrons)
The positive electrode in a fuel cell where oxygen is reduced (gains electrons)
Loss of electrons — hydrogen is oxidised at the anode of a fuel cell
Hydrogen produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity — truly zero-carbon

examTips: Fuel cells produce water as the only product at the point of use — no CO₂ emissions. However always add 'at the point of use' because CO₂ may be produced making the hydrogen.
For evaluation questions on fuel cells: always discuss both advantages (clean, efficient, continuous) AND disadvantages (hydrogen storage, production method, cost, infrastructure).
Remember: hydrogen is oxidised at the anode (OILRIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). State this clearly in exam answers about fuel cell half-equations.
commonMistakes: Saying fuel cells have no environmental disadvantages — hydrogen is currently mostly produced from fossil fuels, so there is still an indirect carbon footprint.
Forgetting that hydrogen is highly flammable and explosive — storage is a genuine safety and engineering challenge.
Confusing the anode and cathode roles — hydrogen goes to the anode (oxidation), oxygen goes to the cathode (reduction).
clozePassages: A hydrogen fuel cell produces electricity by reacting hydrogen and oxygen electrochemically. Hydrogen is supplied to the anode, where it is oxidised, releasing electrons. These electrons flow through an external circuit producing electricity. At the cathode, oxygen is reduced by gaining electrons. The only product is water, making hydrogen fuel cells very clean. They are used in vehicles and portable power supplies.

Fuel cells are more efficient than combustion engines because they convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy without burning fuel. The only waste product when using hydrogen is water. However, most hydrogen is currently produced from natural gas, releasing carbon dioxide. If hydrogen is produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity, fuel cells are truly zero-emission. The challenges include hydrogen storage and the cost of fuel cell technology.

The advantages of hydrogen fuel cells include high efficiency, zero emissions at the point of use, and quiet operation. Disadvantages include the difficulty of storing and transporting hydrogen safely (it is highly flammable), the current high cost of fuel cells, and the fact that most hydrogen production still relies on fossil fuels. Compared to batteries, fuel cells do not run down as long as fuel is supplied, making them suitable for long-distance transport.
